utterances.text: I'm just interested generally if you're aware of such information. If you do, then we could go into more detail if that is something that we would be interested in pursuing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-14
utterances.text: I don't have information, and I wouldn't really like to dwell on any of that because it didn't happen in my village or in my local community. So if some things did happen, perhaps, yes, but I don't feel that I can talk about that then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, I didn't mean for you to comment on anything like that. I just wanted to know if you had heard of any cases like that or not. You can just answer with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-14
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, on the 26th of April, 1992, when Kula Grad fell, as you said, I think that you said at one point that all the neighbouring villages around Zvornik were alerted by radio to surrender and lay down their arms. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-14
utterances.text: I just heard that Kula Grad was liberated. I don't know by whom, how, but this is a broad topic, and of course the propaganda was aimed at letting people know that they need to hand in their weapons and to refrain from putting up any resistance, that there was no point in defending that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And did you hear this over the radio, or did I understand that incorrectly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-14
utterances.text: I don't know if anybody in the village was listening to the radio. I wasn't, but they -- they said that such things were broadcast on the radio. But I heard something else on the radio in a different place. This was around the 30th of May when what happened in our area happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We're still on April. In your statement you say that on the 29th of April, a unit came to your village - I'm not going to mention the name - and that it was, if I understood you correctly, it was a paramilitary formation together with the JNA unit, which was led by a certain Major Pavlovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-14
utterances.text: That unit with that name, it's a man that I don't know. He's a professional soldier. I got that information from people who were there. A unit of the Yugoslav Army came, and they told me that there was a military -- a Yugoslav flag flying on one their military vehicles and that they wanted the weapons to be surrendered in Pod -- Drinjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, if you know, that this Major Pavlovic was a commander of the defence of Zvornik? He was the commander of all the forces in Zvornik. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-14
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know anything about that man at the time. All I knew was what I heard from those people who attended that meeting when the weapons were being handed over. I didn't know anything about him. I just heard some things in stories people were telling during the war and after the war, but I didn't know him at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But that confirms what I said, that he was the commander of all the armed forces. He was the commander of the defence of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-14
utterances.text: I'm going to say what I know. I don't want to comment now about the things that I heard from other people. I'm really not sure. I personally am not sure what he was commander of. I'm not sure. I never really took some information for granted. Some things I wasn't even interested in, who the commander was, I mean, people would say things like that, but as for his name, people who knew him told me what his name was. And he said one thing that I have to mention now. He thanked the people who had brought in and handed over their weapons, and then he personally guaranteed their security in the future, that nothing would happen, meaning that you had become loyal citizens, you can return to your work and your everyday activities, and he thanked the people who had brought in their weapons. I heard that from people who were there. I heard them say that he said that. And they experienced a kind of relief because of that, however, the events that would unfold did not turn out that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We're back in open session. Thank you, sir, for attending, and we wish you a safe journey back to your home. You are now released as a witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is the Prosecution ready with its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the next witness is called I do have an application to make, and I'd ask that we go into closed session for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness is Witness ST-15. Oh, pardon me.
